武田観柳斎.note: A jokin of the Shinsengumi, a rōnin of Izumo learned in warrior usage and military science; a flatterer whom Toshizō despised. He was exposed as a Satsuma informer and cut down within the corps in 1867.

山崎烝.note: The Shinsengumi's chief inspector and intelligence officer, a former physician of Osaka; the corps's ablest scout and shadow.

蒔田相模守広孝.note: Lord of Bitchū-Asao (ten thousand koku) and commander of the Kyoto Mimawarigumi. (The name is sometimes read Maita; the reading follows the source's own gloss.)

戸田采女正氏彬.note: Lord of the Ōgaki domain, a shogunal-loyalist han renowned for its gunnery ('Ōgaki of the guns'). Being ill, he left the field to his deputy Ohara Tesshin.

小原仁兵衛.note: Deputy commander of the Ōgaki troops, pen-name Tesshin; a noted strategist and student of Western gunnery.

太田市之進.note: A Chōshū samurai of the Saga wing who rallied the wavering Fushimi force at Fujinomori; later known as Mihori Kōsuke.

益田越中.note: A Chōshū elder councillor (karō) commanding the Yamazaki wing of the expedition.

児玉民部.note: A Chōshū commander who led the assault on the Shimodachiuri Gate in the Hamaguri Gate battle.

寺島忠三郎.note: A young Chōshū loyalist, close to Kusaka Genzui, with whom he killed himself at the Takatsukasa mansion when the attack failed.

椿弥十郎.note: The Chōshū samurai who distributed the domain's bill of denunciation against the Aizu lord Matsudaira Katamori.

護王神社.note: A shrine facing the west side of the Kyoto Imperial Palace, dedicated to Wake no Kiyomaro; a landmark on the line of the Chōshū advance.

筋違橋.note: A bridge on the road north of Fujinomori, where the Ōgaki troops caught the Chōshū column crossing.

藤ノ森.note: The district and shrine (Fujinomori-myōjin) south of Kyoto, on the Daibutsu highroad, where the Fushimi fighting opened.

鷹司屋敷.note: The Kyoto residence of the Takatsukasa regental house, on the palace's edge, where Kusaka Genzui and Terashima Chūzaburō died.

ch25.note: Marishiten (Sanskrit Mārīci), a Buddhist deity of light and the heat-haze, taken up in Japan as a guardian of warriors and invoked for victory and for the power to vanish from an enemy’s sight. Fighting men carried her image and prayed to her before battle, which is why Kanryūsai’s flattery lands where it does.

The Shinsengumi’s famous standard: the single character makoto (誌), “sincerity” or “fidelity,” in white on a red field. The same character marked the sleeve-bands of the corps’s pale-blue coats. It is the emblem by which the Shinsengumi is remembered.

The Mimawarigumi (“patrol corps”) was the respectable twin of the Shinsengumi: a mounted police force raised from the sons of hatamoto and put under the Kyoto Protector, where the Shinsengumi was a band of commoners and rōnin. Its commander Sasaki Tadasaburō and his men would later be held responsible for the killing of Sakamoto Ryōma.

ch25.anchor: Smite the Aizu Traitors, the Satsuma Rebels
ch25.note: Chōshū carried two standards: the loyalist watchword “Revere the Emperor, Expel the Barbarian” and, beneath it, “Smite the Aizu Traitors and the Satsuma Rebels” (tō-Kai-kan Sasu-zoku). The second named the enemies Chōshū blamed for its expulsion from Kyoto in the coup of the eighth month, 1863: Aizu, which held the city, and Satsuma, then allied with it.

This is the great fire that Kyoto remembered as the Dondon-yaki (also “the gun-fire burning”). Set off by the fighting of the nineteenth to the twenty-first of the seventh month, 1864, it swept the heart of the city and is reckoned to have burned on the order of twenty-eight thousand houses — a catastrophe far outrunning the battle that started it.
